title: Why dance music became a Black specialty
summary: Kmen argues white men had better opportunities, so dance music became a Black trade.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: It seems to me that until the twenties, around in there, the professional jazz musician in New Orleans came definitely from a working class family. And he didn't, uh, maybe have all the advantages of a musical education. I don't know.

I think this fits in though, you see? Just as a, look at it this way. A great many Negroes today, Uh huh. Excel in music, just as they excel in, say, football. Because this is one of the avenues that is open to them, where they can make a mark and go a considerable distance. And this might attract a larger percentage. Let's say that among the whites, there might be a larger percentage having a good deal of native musical ability. But they have opportunities that are so good in the field of law or business or something else. That they channel into that. Now, this was, uh, as I tried to, uh, indicate, I think that before the Civil War, as the war approached, the very profession of, uh, of, uh, playing for dancing came to be, uh, more and more Negro. And then after the Civil War, uh, it got to be almost, uh, a Negro specialty. And due to this, of course, I imagine it would even attract more Negroes in it. He would just go into it as a, as a matter of course. And then White just didn't go into it because he had better opportunities than something else. It wasn't so much just a case of looking down the nose at a musician. When Gottschalk came here in the 1850s, of course, he was a hometown boy, but nevertheless, musicians were idolized that came here. If they were good musicians, they were idolized. When, when Johnny Lynn came here, uh, it was pandemonium. And Barnum actually had to, uh, put a fake Johnny Lynn off the boat in order to draw the crowd away while he got the real Johnny Lynn into her apartment in the Pantavo building. Uh, of course, this was an outstanding attraction, but all visiting musicians were according respect. Mm-hmm. It's just that while you might respect the trade and everything, you wouldn't want your own boy to do it when he could make twice or three times the money in something else or possibly inherit a family business. So just gradually, sort of by default, uh, the, uh, business of providing music for dancing came to, uh, be more and more, especially of the Negro era. But I don't mean to imply that there ever was a time when there weren't white bands and white dance bands.
